title: Crime and Punishment
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
tagline: The whole novel in Constance Garnett’s translation, with one reader’s marginalia.
coverIntro: Below is the novel entire: six parts and an epilogue, every chapter a landing on the trail, colored by its part. The faint arcs are where my notes reach from one chapter to another. Hover a chapter to see what it speaks to; click one and start reading. Sentences underlined in red carry my notes, and each chapter ends with what I make of it. The notes are written for a first reading and do not give away what comes later.
crewIntro: Who is who, with the Russian names untangled. Garnett keeps every patronymic and diminutive, and a first reader can drown in them. The descriptions stop at how each person enters the book and say nothing of what they go on to do.
about: This is the Project Gutenberg text of Constance Garnett’s 1914 translation of Crime and Punishment, unaltered, in its {sections} chapters. Alongside it I have written {essays} chapter readings and pinned {notes} notes to particular sentences. Garnett’s English is Edwardian and sometimes smooths what Dostoevsky left rough. Where a word of hers is doing something odd, a note says so.
Dostoevsky numbered his chapters and gave them no titles. The titles in the chart are mine, added so that the chart can be read. They are a convenience and no part of the book.

The notes are written for someone reading the novel for the first time. It is a book that depends on not knowing, so the notes in a chapter stay inside what you have read so far. Where a link points ahead, it says only that something returns. The persons page keeps the same rule.

On names. Every character has a given name, a patronymic and a surname, and most have a diminutive as well. Rodion Romanovitch Raskolnikov is also Rodya; Avdotya Romanovna is Dounia; Sofya Semyonovna is Sonia. The persons page lists them.

movements.name: Part One
movements.desc: A hot July in Petersburg. A former student, a pawnbroker, a letter from home, and something he calls a rehearsal.

movements.name: Part Two
movements.desc: Fever. The police office, a friend who will not be shaken off, and a visitor from the provinces.

movements.name: Part Three
movements.desc: Family arrives. An article is remembered, and an examining magistrate would like to hear more about it.

movements.name: Part Four
movements.desc: A stranger with a proposal, a reading by candlelight, and a second interview.

movements.name: Part Five
movements.desc: A funeral dinner goes wrong, an accusation is made, and a conversation in a rented room.

movements.name: Part Six
movements.desc: Three men, each with something to offer or to end.

context.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky was born in Moscow in 1821. Arrested for his involvement in socialist circles in 1849, he survived a mock execution and spent four years in a Siberian labor camp. His fiction explores the pressure of moral, political, and religious ideas on individual lives.
context.world: The novel’s Petersburg belongs to a Russia arguing over social change, inherited values, and the place of the individual. Read the characters’ theories alongside their material circumstances: poverty, dependence, and the desire for a way out.
